title: The Soviet Union Responds
subtitle: Stalin speaks while the state mobilizes and the southern front widens
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: A radio address, new reserves and the Prut offensive reveal the distance between German expectations of collapse and the Soviet capacity to continue the war.
body:
On 3 July 1941 Stalin finally addressed the Soviet population about the invasion. Molotov had announced the war eleven days earlier; now the country's dominant political figure spoke in unusually intimate terms, addressing citizens as brothers, sisters and friends. He acknowledged the loss of Lithuania, much of Latvia and extensive territory farther south. He also asserted that Germany's best formations had already been shattered. The admission and the reassurance belonged to the same political undertaking: persuading people to recognize a catastrophe without concluding that resistance was hopeless. The broadcast is valuable precisely because it contains both. It tells us what Stalin wanted his listeners to understand and do, rather than providing an independently reliable account of the fighting.[1]

That morning's argument reached far beyond the radio studio. German headquarters believed the decisive destruction of the Red Army was already substantially accomplished. Soviet headquarters were assembling fresh armies behind those destroyed in the border battles. In the southwest, German and Romanian troops were widening the war across the Prut while Soviet commanders prepared further counterattacks. The question was becoming whether Germany could convert spectacular victories into the collapse of an entire state before that state reorganized its remaining resources. Stalin's speech supplied a public language for that reorganization. Orders, trains, factories and surviving formations would determine how much substance the language acquired.[2]

A speech made necessary by defeat

The broadcast began with a difficulty that propaganda could no longer conceal. Places familiar to Soviet listeners had fallen, and German aircraft were attacking cities well beyond the original frontier. Stalin listed threatened or bombed centres including Smolensk, Kiev, Odessa and Sevastopol. Naming them acknowledged the scale of the emergency while connecting separate local experiences to a common struggle. A person hearing the address in an industrial town or a village did not need to know the composition of a panzer group to understand its central message: the danger was approaching the institutions, homes and livelihoods on which ordinary life depended.[1]

Stalin explained the defeats chiefly through German mobilization, readiness and treachery. The Soviet Union, he maintained, had refused to violate the non-aggression pact and had gained useful preparation time by signing it. This was a defence of his leadership as well as an explanation of events. It omitted the pact's secret territorial arrangements and the Soviet occupations that followed them, already examined in this atlas's study of 23 August 1939. It also avoided a public accounting of the readiness decisions that had left Soviet formations vulnerable. Germany's responsibility for launching this invasion did not make Stalin's account of his own diplomacy complete.[1][3]

His assertion that the finest German divisions had met their destruction was reassurance rather than an audited military finding. The German army was suffering casualties and confronting stubborn resistance, but its principal striking forces remained capable of further operations. The speech offered no unit list or casualty assessment that could substantiate its sweeping claim. Reading it alongside the German situation sheet for 3 July makes the tension clear: the map depicts an invasion still advancing on several axes, while the broadcast insists that the invader's apparent invincibility has already been broken. Both documents have perspectives; neither should be allowed to authenticate itself.[1][4]

Yet the address did more than disguise failure. Stalin explicitly demanded an end to complacency and a complete reorientation of civilian work. He treated the war as a struggle for collective survival and called for assistance to the wounded, protection of communications, increased weapons production and reinforcement of the army. These were practical categories of activity. They offered listeners roles beyond waiting for a communiqué or fearing an approaching tank column. The speech's force lay partly in this connection between an immense national danger and specific work that could be organized locally.[1]

Who was now directing the war?

The machinery of command had begun changing before Stalin spoke. On 23 June the government established the Stavka of the High Command, a central military headquarters chaired by Defence Commissar Semyon Timoshenko. Stalin was a member, alongside senior military and political leaders. His political supremacy and Timoshenko's formal chairmanship were therefore different facts. Calling Stalin supreme commander from the first day of the invasion obscures the stages by which authority was reorganized during the summer. For this date, the important point is that military direction was already being concentrated, while its relationship with Stalin's personal power remained less straightforward than later retrospective diagrams suggest.[2]

The State Defence Committee, usually identified by its Russian initials GKO, followed on 30 June under Stalin's chairmanship. Its remit extended beyond directing armies to mobilizing the state's economic and administrative resources. A new committee could not restore an army's missing radios or recover an abandoned ammunition depot. It could, however, establish a political authority capable of issuing decisions across institutions whose normal responsibilities competed: defence, transport, industrial production and internal security. Stalin announced this concentration of authority in the broadcast, presenting it as the organizational counterpart to his demand for a collective national effort.[5][1]

At the front, rebuilding command meant more than establishing committees in Moscow. The Western Front had lost much of its original force and communications system. Timoshenko took over its direction in early July, and reserve armies were being brought toward the Western Dvina–Dnieper region. This placed the immediate problem in a different geographical setting from the Białystok salient. The next defence had to be constructed around river crossings and the approaches to Vitebsk, Orsha and Smolensk, using formations that had not all been destroyed in the frontier battles. Germany's success against one deployment was forcing the Soviets to create another.[2]

There was nevertheless no clean transition from confusion to competence. New headquarters inherited incomplete information, unfamiliar formations and urgent orders. The ability to send a directive should not be mistaken for the ability to coordinate every recipient. The counterstrokes of the previous week had demonstrated the price of mistimed concentration; similar problems would recur. What changed was the scale on which the Soviet leadership was attempting to replace losses and organize resistance. Its response was neither a fully functioning master plan nor administrative paralysis. Both descriptions remove the difficult work being performed between those extremes.[2]

A headquarters is not a cabinet

Stavka directed military operations; the GKO exercised emergency authority across the state. Stalin's leading position in both systems developed through separate appointments. On 3 July he chaired the GKO, while the original Stavka had been established under Timoshenko. Treating the two organizations as interchangeable hides how the Soviet response was being assembled.[2][5]

The reserves behind the broken armies

The German assumption of imminent victory rested partly on identifying the army in front of the Wehrmacht with the total military capacity of the Soviet Union. Destroying the western formations was an enormous achievement, but it did not automatically dispose of the reserves farther east. The Soviet mobilization decree of 22 June applied to fourteen military districts and called up the designated reserve age groups. Ziemke and Bauer's official military history reports that 5.3 million men had been mobilized by 1 July. That is a measure of administrative and human mobilization, not a claim that 5.3 million trained, equipped combat soldiers had appeared at the front.[6][2]

A replacement army required weapons, transport, staffs, medical services and time to organize its units. The distinction matters especially after losses of heavy equipment and experienced personnel. Mobilized men could replenish a formation only if they could reach it and be incorporated into a functioning structure. A headquarters receiving divisions from the interior still had to establish their positions, distribute instructions and provide supplies. The presence of large reserves therefore offered possibilities rather than an immediate remedy. Germany had good reason to value the destruction of Soviet equipment and formations, even though it exaggerated how completely those losses had exhausted Soviet resistance.[2]

The emerging defensive scheme concentrated important reserves in the centre. Four armies comprising thirty-seven divisions were assigned to the Dnieper–Western Dvina region in the reconstruction summarized by Ziemke and Bauer. The northern forces were to prepare resistance around the approaches to Pskov, while the Southwestern Front and the adjacent part of the Southern Front were to use the older fortified frontier. These were distinct responses to distinct operational dangers. The surviving forces in Ukraine retained more organizational coherence than the shattered western armies, while the Baltic withdrawals exposed routes toward Leningrad. A single order to stand everywhere would not have answered all three problems.[2]

Defensive organization also retained an offensive element. Soviet commanders sought to interrupt the German advance through counterstrokes, rather than simply occupying a succession of fixed lines. The Lepel operation being prepared in the centre and the counterattack orders on the Prut belonged to that approach. Their prospects depended on concentration, reconnaissance and cooperation among formations, precisely the capabilities that had proved fragile in June. Continued Soviet activity therefore did not establish that the recovery would be successful. It established that the enemy whom German headquarters considered decisively beaten was still making operational choices.[7][8]

Removing what the invader needed

Evacuation gave strategic depth a practical meaning. The government had created an Evacuation Council on 24 June, and a decree of 25 June addressed the transfer of equipment and core personnel from newly established aviation-industry plants in Riga, Tallinn, Mogilev, Minsk and Dnepropetrovsk. These records show that evacuation was already an administrative undertaking before Stalin's broadcast. They do not show that every listed factory was successfully removed. The speed of the invasion made the difference between issuing instructions and loading machinery onto trains painfully important.[9][6]

The speech translated that policy into a stark general rule. When troops withdrew, railway engines and wagons were to be taken away, cattle driven east, and grain and fuel removed or destroyed. Stalin extended the instruction to valuable industrial materials. Its military logic was clear: territory should not become an intact source of food, transport and production for the invading army. But implementing it required the same scarce resources needed by the front. Railway capacity could not simultaneously carry every reinforcement westward and every endangered workshop eastward. Even where an instruction was obeyed, the result could be dislocation as well as preservation.[1]

The relationship between evacuation and destruction was particularly harsh for civilians. A cow, a grain store or a railway wagon was a strategic resource to a headquarters and an immediate means of survival to a household. Destroying what could not be removed denied material to the enemy, but it could also leave people who remained with less to eat and fewer ways to escape. That consequence follows directly from the policy; it does not require imagining that every locality experienced an identical, efficiently executed scorched-earth programme. The speech gave an instruction. The circumstances of particular withdrawals determined which property could be saved, abandoned or destroyed.[1]

Stalin also called for partisan detachments and sabotage behind German lines, specifying bridges, roads, communications and stores as targets. This was an attempt to turn the invader's growing rear into another field of war. It was not evidence that a coordinated partisan network already covered the occupied regions. Organization, weapons, local support and contact with Soviet authorities all had to be established. The immediate significance of the broadcast was its authorization of continued struggle beyond the moving front, together with the insistence that occupation did not end the population's obligations to the Soviet state.[1]

Patriotic mobilization remained bound to coercion. Stalin demanded severe action against deserters, people accused of spreading panic, spies and supposed saboteurs, and called for military tribunals. Such language could mobilize resolve while also encouraging suspicion. The speech did not abolish the habits or institutions of Stalinist rule; it applied them to a national emergency. Recognizing the danger of Nazi conquest does not require presenting the Soviet response as free of repression. Nor does recognizing repression explain away the genuine reasons millions had to defend their families and communities against the invasion.[1]

A new offensive across the Prut

While attention centred on Minsk and the central rivers, the southern end of the front was entering a more active phase. The main German–Romanian offensive across the Prut began on 2 July. Romania's immediate territorial objective was the recovery of Bessarabia and northern Bukovina, lost to the Soviet Union in 1940. German planning connected operations from Romania to the wider campaign against Soviet forces west of the Dnieper. The Prut was therefore both a contested frontier and the starting line for a manoeuvre intended to affect the armies withdrawing through Ukraine.[10][11]

Eugen von Schobert's German Eleventh Army supplied the principal German command on this wing of Gerd von Rundstedt's Army Group South. Romanian armies operated alongside it under Ion Antonescu's national leadership; the Fourth Army, commanded by Nicolae Ciupercă, covered the more southerly Prut sector. The Romanian Third Army's assignment on 3 July was to cross between Cernăuți and Noua Suliță and continue toward Hotin on the Dniester. Cernăuți is present-day Chernivtsi, and Hotin is Khotyn. These objectives describe the northern Bukovinian and Bessarabian approach, not a completed sweep to the Black Sea.[11][10]

Facing this offensive, the Soviet Southern Front under Ivan Tyulenev had to defend the approaches from Romania while maintaining contact with the Southwestern Front farther north. Its Ninth Army's counterattack order offers a closer view than the broad campaign arrows. It described enemy crossings near the Costești–Sculeni sector and directed a right-wing grouping to destroy the forces that had entered Soviet-held territory and restore the frontier between Lopatnik and Sculeni. The objective remained local and ambitious: eliminate the bridgeheads before their occupants could spread farther into Bessarabia.[12][8]

The Second Mechanized Corps was to strike through the Nicoreni–Moșeni–Bărate(n) area against the penetration near Zaicani and prevent the enemy's withdrawal across the Prut. The Forty-Eighth Rifle Corps received a converging task, while elements of the Thirtieth Rifle Division were to protect the flank against forces approaching from Sculeni. Aviation was assigned to attack crossings and suppress artillery on the river's western bank. This combination of tanks, infantry, flank protection and attacks on bridges reveals a coherent conception. Whether all those elements could act together is a separate question, and the document cannot prove it.[8]

The order specified an attack at 16:00 on 4 July and demanded reports of readiness, the beginning of the attack and subsequent progress every two hours. Those requirements expose what a successful defence needed: information moving back from subordinate formations while instructions moved forward. They also provide a real timetable against which later events could be examined. There is no equivalent basis here for declaring that the whole Axis offensive was a fixed number of days late. On 3 July the immediate contest was still over bridgeheads, approaches and the capacity to concentrate against them. The Dniester and the larger Ukrainian envelopment remained objectives beyond the current fighting.[8][11]

An order with conflicting dates

The published Ninth Army order is headed 3 July at 01:40, describes events “by the end” of 3 July, gives an aviation task for 1 July and schedules the attack for 4 July. These internal inconsistencies may reflect errors in the document or its transmission. The order establishes the intended counterstroke, but cannot securely establish the hour at which every reported position became known.[8]

The violence behind the southern front

The Romanian rear had already become a site of mass murder. At Iași, killings and arrests on 28–29 June were followed by the deportation of Jewish survivors in sealed freight trains. The International Commission on the Holocaust in Romania identified Romanian military, police and intelligence institutions as central perpetrators, with German military participation. False allegations about Jewish signalling and attacks supplied a supposed security rationale. The Commission distinguishes this operation from the activities of Einsatzgruppe D: that formation did not carry out the Iași pogrom. Identifying the actual institutions matters more than assigning every massacre to the most familiar Nazi organization.[13]

The trains made transport itself an instrument of killing. A photograph dated 1 July records Roma removing bodies during a stop at Târgu Frumos on the Iași–Călărași route. Its archival description identifies the overcrowded, unventilated wagons and summer heat that killed hundreds during the transports, which had left Iași on 30 June. This is a specific episode, not a generic illustration of later deportations. It places civilian persecution beside the military timetable of the offensive beginning across the nearby Prut.[14]

Iași was within Romania, not territory newly conquered from the Soviet Union. Its importance to the campaign lies partly in that geography. Violence did not simply appear after a victorious army entered an enemy town; an allied state used the emergency of war to persecute and murder people already under its authority. Security language connected the alleged internal enemy to the external military struggle. The international Commission's reconstruction supports responsibility at the level of institutions and participants rather than the misleading explanation of an uncontrollable crowd acting alone.[13]

Stalin's assertion that invasion threatened whole peoples must therefore be assessed on two levels. His account of Soviet freedom and his diplomatic innocence was propaganda. The danger posed by the invading coalition to civilians, especially Jews, was real and already being demonstrated. The evidence does not need either government's public narrative to become intelligible. It requires attention to the particular orders, perpetrators and victims in each place. For a reader following the Prut offensive, the killings at Iași are part of the same historical moment as the bridgeheads and army orders, without being reducible to an outcome of combat.

Allies promised and assistance negotiated

Stalin also acknowledged Churchill's offer of support and the American government's declared readiness to help. His language placed Soviet resistance within a wider struggle against Hitler, despite the recent hostility between Moscow and the Western powers. The practical beginnings of cooperation were more tentative than this public alignment might suggest. In Washington on 26 June, Sumner Welles told Soviet ambassador Konstantin Umansky that requests for material assistance would receive attention, but would have to be considered alongside American defence needs and existing help to Britain and other victims of German aggression.[1][15]

That conversation reveals the unglamorous foundations of an alliance. Welles pointed to the release of blocked Soviet funds and the decision not to issue a neutrality proclamation for the German–Soviet war. Umansky raised pending export licences and the shortage of shipping. He mentioned Soviet cargo vessels on the Pacific coast that could carry supplies to Vladivostok, while admitting that the requirement was greater than the available tonnage. These were already concrete issues, but they were not equivalent to weapons delivered to an army fighting on the Berezina or the Prut.[15]

The following day's meeting with Dean Acheson was similarly practical. Umansky presented lists of goods and asked for a simpler way to deal with the necessary American agencies. Acheson explained that a coordinating committee had been established. The ambassador subsequently corrected his own claim that all listed equipment was finished and available: a crane had been requisitioned, and pumps for destroyers were only partly completed. This small correction is useful evidence of what early cooperation actually involved. Before assistance could become a strategic fact, officials had to determine what existed, who controlled it, whether it could be exported and how it could be moved.[16]

The alliance began with inventories

A crane and unfinished destroyer pumps appear in the American record of 27 June. They are a reminder that declarations of solidarity and usable military assistance operated on different timescales. The memorandum records an application and a correction, not a completed shipment to the Soviet front.[16]

Two incompatible readings of the same war

On 3 July Franz Halder concluded that the campaign had, in its decisive military sense, already been won in less than a fortnight. His reasoning rested on the destruction of Soviet armies west of the Dvina and Dnieper. He still expected further fighting and the occupation of immense territory; his judgment was not that every Soviet soldier had surrendered. It was that Germany had removed the principal organized obstacle, leaving the denial of industrial resources and the defeat of lesser surviving forces as the remaining work. The distinction explains how a knowledgeable chief of staff could recognize continuing resistance while drawing a profoundly premature conclusion.[2][11]

The evidence available by this date justified neither Soviet triumphalism nor German certainty. Germany had destroyed formations, taken major cities and forced withdrawals on a vast scale. The Soviet Union had retained a government able to mobilize, a command apparatus capable of creating new groupings, and armies still able to resist and counterattack. None of those facts guaranteed survival. Together they made the assumption of completed strategic victory unsafe. Stalin's address matters in this setting as a declaration that the state intended to organize a longer war, not as the moment when that longer war was already secured.[2][1]

The next test would occur beyond the catastrophe at Minsk. Fresh Soviet formations were preparing to strike toward Lepel while German armour approached the river corridor leading to Smolensk. The study for 6 July follows that collision. It would show both the continuing Soviet capacity to put substantial forces into action and the immense difficulty of using them effectively against an enemy whose operational momentum remained formidable.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link to the source list and return to their first use. Page and document references accompany the relevant notes. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
